subject: Cox Proportional Hazard model - multiple declarations for a node

messages.author: d2611f73e03a1fcd
messages.subject: Cox Proportional Hazard model - multiple declarations for a node
parts:
Hey everyone,

I am struggling to get a Cox Proportional Hazard model up and running in nimble. I am using bugs code for reference that has been implemented multiple times in other papers, but I am getting an error for multiple declarations of a node.

Here is the model code:

nimble::nimbleCode({

#n = number of individuals

#t = the time step

  for(b in 1:Nbeta){

    beta[b] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)

  }

  for(i in 1:n){

    for(k in 1:t){

      # risk set = 1 if obs.t >= t

      Y[i,k] <- step(obs.t[i] - t.int[k] + eps)

      # counting process jump = 1 if obs.t is within interval

      dN[i,k] <- Y[i,k] * step(t.int[k + 1] - obs.t[i] - eps) * delta[i]

    }

  }

  # Model

  for(k in 1:t){

    for(i in 1:n){

      dN[i,k] ~ dpois(idt[i,k]) # likelihood

      idt[i,k] <- Y[i,k] * exp(LinearPred[i]) * dL0[k] # intensity

      # linear predictors

      LinearPred[i] <- beta[1]*X[i,1] + beta[2]*X[i,2] + beta[3]*X[i,3] + beta[4]*X[i,4]

    }

    dL0[k] <- dgamma(0.01, 0.01)

    # Survivor function = exp(-Integral{l0(u)du})^exp(beta*z)

    S[k] <- pow(exp(-sum(dL0[1:k])), exp(LinearPred[i] * -0.5))

    }

  })

I am getting the multiple declarations error for dN. I understand that I am defining dN twice; however, I am attempting to first deterministically define dN in the first chunk then use dN for a likelihood function as data to estimate idt and the other parameters. I will admit that I have not run this in winBugs, but the model structure is used in multiple different papers. Is there anyway to make this work in nimble?

messages.author: f116cbe5c604c988
messages.subject: Re: Cox Proportional Hazard model - multiple declarations for a node
parts:
Anthony, thanks for using nimble, and also for sending this question.

Yes, you're correct that nimble does not allow *both* stochastic (~) and deterministic (<-) declarations of the same node.  Using both would invariably lead to some ambiguity, for example:

x <- a + b
x ~ dnorm(0, 1)

Should the value of x be fixed to be consistently equal to "a + b" ?
If x is not specified as data, then should this non-data node be sampled from a dnorm(0,1) distribution?  Sampling of x would likely be inconsistent with the value "a+b", leading to a contradiction.
If x is specified as data, and a data value is provided, then that value is likely different from the value "a+b", leading to another contradiction.

So, in the design of nimble, we do not allow this case.

I can understand one use-case here, which is the following: As in the example above, you want the value of "a+b" to contribute to the likelihood, being evaluated as compared to a dnorm(0,1) distribution.  In this case, you could achieve this in nimble using a custom distribution, as:

dMyDist <- nimbleFunction(
   run = function(x = double(), theta = double(), log = integer()) {    ## "y" will take the place of "x", and "a+b" will take the place of "theta"
      lp <- dnorm(theta, 0, 1)    ## you could use any distribution here, in your case dpois()      
      returnType(double())
      if(log) return(lp) else return(exp(lp))
   }
)

code <- nimbleCode({
   ...
   y ~ dMyDist(theta = a + b)
})

## definitely specify a data value for y, so the model does not try to simulate it
data <- list(y = 0)    ## the data value you provide for y does not matter.  It will be used as "x" in the custom distribution (which is never used)

This code above should get you running, if your desired use-case is the one described above.  Let me know if you need help modifying the code above for your specific model.  In your model, you would also need to pass the value "idt[i,k]" as a second argument into the dMyDist function, perhaps named "theta2" or any other name you want.

As a final note, I think you'll also get a multiple declarations error from your declaration of LinearPred[i], which is contained inside both loops:

for(k in 1:t){
    for(i in 1:n){

So, unless LinearPred is also indexed by k (for example: LinearPred[i,k] <- ...), your model will also result in multiple declarations for LinearPred[i].  It might be a simple matter of changing the nesting of your for-loops a little bit, so the declaration LinearPred[i] only appears in one loop: for(i in 1:n).

Hope this helps, and keep at it,
Daniel
